Thank you all so much for your hard work and development of this software. In this post I'm making a feature request and asking a few questions

I'm running several large models with loads of data, and would like to compare these models using WAIC. 
Using thin/thin2 I've been able to obtain WAIC values on a simple model. Unfortunately, with more complex models, WAIC returns as NaN with the suggestion of tracing latent states. If I do trace latent states, this will break down when nimble tries to return the latent state nodes because this array is too large for R. Would it be possible to trace latent states for the purpose of computing WAIC within c++, without having that object returned to R (since that's where it breaks). The models compile and run otherwise. Is WAIC computed prior to thinning? Is it computed using the minimum size if thin/thin2 are different?

Also, because of the size of both the models and data, ideally we'd run them with parallel chains. This brings up a few questions: 
1. If we do run the chains in parallel, seems like we won't be able to compute WAIC using all samples from all chains, similar to how the nimbleMCMC function does, unless we do it manually (feature request implied)
2. I've seen on other posts that we need to compile the model and mcmc seperately. Does this include building and configuring the mcmc? I have gotten it to run and return samples with just compiling the mcmc. However, when returning the compiled/run object, i.e. Cmcmc, this causes R to segfault and crash. I've gotten a few error messages including: 
    A."Error in .Call(NULL, <pointer: (nil)>) : first argument must be a string (of length 1) or native symbol reference", 
    B. > samples<- as.matrix(mcmcout[[1]]$mvSamples)
        Error: Sextptr is not a valid external pointer
        
        *** caught segfault ***
        address (nil), cause 'memory not mapped'

It works to extract the samples seperately and return them, but then that seperate chain WAIC problem pops up.

  mu ~ dnorm(0, 1)
  for(i in 1:100){
    x[i] ~ dnorm(mu, 1)
    y[i] ~ dnorm(x[i], 1)
  }
})
Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code, data = list(y = y))
conf <- configureMCMC(Rmodel,monitors=c("mu"))
Rmcmc <- buildMCMC(conf, enableWAIC = TRUE)
Cmodel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)

On Fri, Mar 29, 2019 at 8:49 AM Alison Ketz <aliso...@gmail.com> wrote:
Thank you all so much for your hard work and development of this software. In this post I'm making a feature request and asking a few questions

I'm running several large models with loads of data, and would like to compare these models using WAIC. 
Using thin/thin2 I've been able to obtain WAIC values on a simple model. Unfortunately, with more complex models, WAIC returns as NaN with the suggestion of tracing latent states. If I do trace latent states, this will break down when nimble tries to return the latent state nodes because this array is too large for R. Would it be possible to trace latent states for the purpose of computing WAIC within c++, without having that object returned to R (since that's where it breaks). The models compile and run otherwise. Is WAIC computed prior to thinning? Is it computed using the minimum size if thin/thin2 are different?

First, some preliminaries: Are you up to date on nimble?  There was a bug fix a couple of versions or so back in which WAIC could fail when combining multiple chains.  If that is the source of your NaN, it might be resolved simply by updating nimble.

No, the WAIC does not currently work just within C++.  

WAIC should be post-thinning.  No, there is not a clever combination of thin and thin2.  WAIC is calculated from the monitors with thin, not the monitors2 with thin2.  I think you could make the more highly thinned case be monitors and thin, with everything you need for WAIC.  If you want a less thinned sample without latent states, you could do that in monitors2 and thin2.

Also, because of the size of both the models and data, ideally we'd run them with parallel chains. This brings up a few questions: 
1. If we do run the chains in parallel, seems like we won't be able to compute WAIC using all samples from all chains, similar to how the nimbleMCMC function does, unless we do it manually (feature request implied)

That is correct.  You could do the following: After running chains in parallel (see below), append samples from all chains into the mvSamples of one of the Cmcmc objects.  Then, call its calculateWAIC method.  To append the chains together, first append them in an R matrix, using for example rbind.  Then do nimble:::matrix2mv(posteriorSamplesMatrix, Cmcmc$mvSamples), where posteriorSamplesMatrix is the matrix of combined samples. This will copy posteriorSamplesMatrix into Cmcmc$mvSamples, from which WAIC is calculated.  See source code for runMCMC for an example of this maneuver.  The "nimble:::" is necessary because matrix2mv is not an exported package function because there hasn't been a use case like this before, but maybe it should be.

2. I've seen on other posts that we need to compile the model and mcmc seperately. Does this include building and configuring the mcmc? I have gotten it to run and return samples with just compiling the mcmc. However, when returning the compiled/run object, i.e. Cmcmc, this causes R to segfault and crash. I've gotten a few error messages including:

Yes, you need to start with a new model object and a new MCMC object in each thread and compile them in each thread. (Actually, they can be compiled in a single call to compileNimble, which will return a list, but I think people typically do them in two calls.  But that's not really the nub of your question.) The errors you report could come from not doing so.  From what you did, the multiple compiled MCMCs may have run and returned samples, but they would have been using the same compiled model object, creating mayhem and results that should not be trusted, as well as the kind of crash you report.  Improving capability to parallelize is a big design goal but one that will take some time.

There is one step of the process where you can save processing.  Once you have an uncompiled model object, say Rmodel, then Rmodel$newModel(replicate=TRUE) should return a new model object with all the same content as the old one.  As always, using check=FALSE (may be default) and calculate=FALSE will save some time.

I hope it all helps.  Thanks for the questions.

The core developers are spread out among trips, so further answers may be slower than usual in the next week or two.

-Perry
